title: A critical role of ocean–sea ice interactions in the pronounced warmth during the Miocene Climatic Optimum
abstract: The Miocene Climatic Optimum was characterized by global mean temperatures 8-10 °C above the preindustrial level, yet such extreme warmth remains difficult to reproduce in climate models. Using two climate models (IPSL-CM5A2 and NorESM1-F) with updated boundary conditions, we show that the simulated climate of this interval strongly depends on ocean-ice dynamics. The NorESM1-F model produces surface temperatures more consistent with proxy reconstructions, driven by a stronger overturning circulation, enhanced poleward heat and salt transport, and near-permanent sea-ice loss. In contrast, IPSL-CM5A2 simulates a weaker overturning circulation and limited polar amplification, which is generally consistent with previous modeling results. Our results suggest that the Miocene Climatic Optimum may represent a distinct high-latitude climate regime, emphasizing the critical role of ocean–ice feedbacks in driving the strong polar amplification and the necessity of multi-model comparisons together with proxy constraints to understand the climate of this interval. Ocean-ice interactions play a pivotal role in amplification of polar climate change, as demonstrated by contrasting results for the magnitude of northern high-latitude warming during the Miocene Climatic Optimum from NorESM1-F and IPSL-CM5A2 climate models
problem: Existing climate models struggle to reproduce the extreme warmth and strong polar amplification characteristic of the Miocene Climatic Optimum, with the mechanisms responsible, particularly the critical role of ocean-sea ice interactions, remaining unclear.
method: This study investigates the climate of the Miocene Climatic Optimum using two Earth System Models with updated paleogeography and varying CO2 levels to systematically assess the critical role of ocean-sea ice interactions in driving the period's pronounced warmth and polar amplification.
task: The task is to investigate the role of ocean-sea ice interactions in the pronounced warmth of the Miocene Climatic Optimum by comparing climate simulations from two different Earth System Models (NorESM1-F and IPSL-CM5A2) and analyzing their divergent results.

Two additional experiments with Atmospheric General Circulation Model (AGCM) are conducted to evaluate the contribution of sea ice and SSTs on the warming differences in the NH high latitudes between two models. The applied AGCM is kept the same version and same resolution as in the NorESM1-F (CAM4, f19).

For the MCO experiments, the runoff settings utilize the native river routing schemes embedded within each model's land surface model. The NorESM1-F model employs the scheme within CLM471,72, while the IPSL-CM5A2 model uses the one in ORCHIDEE73,74.

In the Atlantic (Fig. 5a-d), the North Atlantic current in MCO simulation is more confined to the western boundaries south of 60°N before flowing northward to the Nordic Seas in the NorESM experiment, where the subpolar gyre nearly disappears, allowing most of the warm North Atlantic water to reach the Arctic Ocean.

In the Atlantic (Fig. 5a-d), the North Atlantic current in MCO simulation is more confined to the western boundaries south of 60°N before flowing northward to the Nordic Seas in the NorESM experiment, where the subpolar gyre nearly disappears, allowing most of the warm North Atlantic water to reach the Arctic Ocean.

In the Pacific Ocean (Fig. 5e-h), we observe a pronounced northward expansion of the subtropical gyre in the NorESM MCO simulation relative to its modern condition, allowing warm western boundary currents to flow further north, potentially transporting more heat to the subpolar region of the North Pacific (Fig. 5f).

Another important difference located in the South Pacific, e.g. a notable retro flow is observed in the western tropical Indo-Pacific in the MCO simulation by NorESM model, where the westward Pacific tropical current first flows to the Indian Ocean before retro-flowing south-eastward along northeast Australia and finally joining the ACC in the Southern Ocean.
